title: New in London
synopsis: You've just moved to London to study. Survive a broken ticket, a packed coffee shop and your first job interview, using only your English.

vocab.meaning: a polite way to get someone's attention (or to get past them)
vocab.example: Excuse me, is this seat free?
vocab.exampleTranslation: Sorry to bother you: can I sit here?

vocab.meaning: a card or piece of paper that lets you travel or go in somewhere
vocab.example: I need a ticket to Camden Town.
vocab.exampleTranslation: I must pay to travel to Camden Town.

vocab.meaning: is broken, or is not accepted
vocab.example: The coffee machine doesn't work.
vocab.exampleTranslation: The coffee machine is broken.

vocab.meaning: in or to what place (a question word)
vocab.example: Where is the bus stop?
vocab.exampleTranslation: In what place is the bus stop?

vocab.meaning: what price, or what amount (for things you can't count)
vocab.example: How much is this sandwich?
vocab.exampleTranslation: What does this sandwich cost?

vocab.meaning: a one-way ticket (UK English); the opposite of a return
vocab.example: A single to Oxford, please.
vocab.exampleTranslation: A one-way ticket to Oxford, please.

vocab.meaning: UK money (£). £2.80 = 'two pounds eighty'
vocab.example: It costs five pounds.
vocab.exampleTranslation: The price is £5.

vocab.meaning: the place next to the tracks where you get on a train
vocab.example: The train leaves from platform four.
vocab.exampleTranslation: Get on the train at platform 4.

vocab.meaning: a train route with a name, like the Northern line
vocab.example: Take the Central line to Oxford Circus.
vocab.exampleTranslation: Use the train route called 'Central'.

vocab.meaning: going north (-bound = travelling towards: southbound, eastbound, westbound)
vocab.example: The northbound train is late.
vocab.exampleTranslation: The train going north is late.

vocab.meaning: be careful of the space between the train and the platform
vocab.example: Mind the gap when you get off.
vocab.exampleTranslation: Be careful of the space when you leave the train.

vocab.meaning: an apartment (UK English)
vocab.example: My flat is on the third floor.
vocab.exampleTranslation: My apartment is on the third floor.

vocab.meaning: a line of people waiting (UK English)
vocab.example: There's a long queue at the bakery.
vocab.exampleTranslation: Many people are waiting in line at the bakery.

vocab.meaning: staff asking 'What would you like?'
vocab.example: Hi! What can I get you?
vocab.exampleTranslation: Hi! What would you like to order?

vocab.meaning: coffee made with a lot of hot milk
vocab.example: A large latte, please.
vocab.exampleTranslation: A big milky coffee, please.

vocab.meaning: a polite way to order or ask for something
vocab.example: Could I have the bill, please?
vocab.exampleTranslation: Please bring me the bill.

vocab.meaning: to take food or drink with you, not have it there (US: 'to go')
vocab.example: Two coffees to take away, please.
vocab.exampleTranslation: Two coffees that I'll take with me, please.

vocab.meaning: to eat or drink it in the café (US: 'for here')
vocab.example: Is that to have in?
vocab.exampleTranslation: Will you drink it here?

vocab.meaning: something more (staff ask: 'Anything else?')
vocab.example: Anything else for you today?
vocab.exampleTranslation: Do you want something more today?

vocab.meaning: nothing more, thanks
vocab.example: No, that's all, thanks.
vocab.exampleTranslation: I don't need anything more.

vocab.meaning: to give something to someone for a short time
vocab.example: Could you lend me your pen?
vocab.exampleTranslation: Can I use your pen for a moment?

vocab.meaning: to take something from someone for a short time
vocab.example: Can I borrow your umbrella?
vocab.exampleTranslation: Can I use your umbrella and give it back later?

vocab.meaning: not having enough money right now
vocab.example: I'm a bit short this month.
vocab.exampleTranslation: I don't have enough money this month.

vocab.meaning: a casual way to say 'How are you?'
vocab.example: Hey, how's it going?
vocab.exampleTranslation: Hi, how are you?

vocab.meaning: with each other
vocab.example: Let's study together.
vocab.exampleTranslation: Let's study with each other.

vocab.meaning: worried and a little afraid before something important
vocab.example: I always get nervous before exams.
vocab.exampleTranslation: I feel worried before exams.

vocab.meaning: happy and full of energy about something (the -ing form 'exciting' = causing that feeling)
vocab.example: I'm so excited about the trip!
vocab.exampleTranslation: I'm really happy and can't wait for the trip!

vocab.meaning: a formal meeting where someone asks you questions, e.g. for a job
vocab.example: I have a job interview tomorrow.
vocab.exampleTranslation: Tomorrow I meet an employer who may give me a job.

vocab.meaning: the person in charge of a shop or a team
vocab.example: Can I speak to the manager?
vocab.exampleTranslation: Can I talk to the person in charge?

vocab.meaning: a polite thing to say when you meet someone for the first time
vocab.example: Hi, I'm Tom. Nice to meet you!
vocab.exampleTranslation: Hello, I'm Tom. I'm happy to meet you.

vocab.meaning: people who buy things in a shop
vocab.example: We have lots of customers on Saturdays.
vocab.exampleTranslation: Many people come to buy things on Saturdays.

vocab.meaning: the money you get for work
vocab.example: The pay is good at this café.
vocab.exampleTranslation: This café gives good money for work.

vocab.meaning: to begin
vocab.example: When can you start?
vocab.exampleTranslation: From when can you begin work?

vocab.meaning: lessons that teach you how to do a job
vocab.example: New staff get two days of training.
vocab.exampleTranslation: New workers learn the job for two days.

vocab.meaning: a period of work time, e.g. 9am to 2pm
vocab.example: My shift starts at nine.
vocab.exampleTranslation: I begin work at nine.

vocab.meaning: a polite way to ask for information
vocab.example: Could you tell me where the station is?
vocab.exampleTranslation: Please tell me where the station is.

episodes.title: Mind the Gap
episodes.goal: Get from the station to your new flat in Camden Town.
episodes.synopsis: Day 1. Your ticket won't open the gate, and the station is packed. A station assistant is your only hope.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Day 1. You've just arrived in London to study. Your new flat is in Camden Town, a few stops away.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: At the busy station, you touch your ticket on the gate… Beep! The gate stays closed.

lines.speaker: you
lines.text: Oh no… my ticket doesn't work!
lines.reading: oh NO… my TICK-et DOESN'T WORK!
lines.translation: Oh no, the gate won't accept my ticket!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A station assistant in a navy cap and uniform is standing by the gates. Time to get his attention.

choices.translation: (Polite) Can I talk to you, please?
choices.feedback: 'Excuse me' is the polite way to get a stranger's attention.
choices.why: 'Excuse me' opens a conversation with someone you don't know: staff, people in the street, anyone. 'Sorry' is mainly for apologising, and 'Hey!' sounds rude to strangers.

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: Hello there! Can I help you?
reaction.reading: hel-LO there! can I HELP you?
reaction.translation: Hi! Do you need help?

choices.feedback: 'Hey, you!' sounds rude and demanding to a stranger. Use 'Excuse me'.
choices.why: 'Hey' is fine with friends, but 'Hey, you!' to staff sounds angry, as if you're telling them off. 'Excuse me' gets attention politely.

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: Er… yes? Next time, just say 'excuse me'! How can I help?
reaction.reading: ER… YES? NEXT TIME, just say ex-CUSE me! HOW can I HELP?
reaction.translation: Um, yes? Please be polite next time. What do you need?

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: A few people in the queue turn round to look at you.

choices.feedback: 'Thank you' is for after someone helps you. To start a conversation, say 'Excuse me'.
choices.why: In English, 'thank you' comes after help: 'Thank you for your help!' Before anything has happened, use 'Excuse me' to start talking.

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: You're welcome… but I haven't done anything yet!
reaction.reading: you're WEL-come… but I HAVEN'T done AN-y-thing YET!
reaction.translation: No problem… but I haven't helped you yet!

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: So, how can I help?
reaction.reading: SO, HOW can I HELP?
reaction.translation: What do you need?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He waits for you to explain the problem.

choices.translation: There's a problem: the gate won't accept my ticket.
choices.feedback: Simple and clear: 'My ticket doesn't work' explains exactly what's wrong.
choices.why: 'Doesn't work' is the everyday way to say something is broken or not accepted: 'My card doesn't work', 'The lift doesn't work'. Present-tense negatives use do/does + not + verb.

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: Let me have a look… Ah, this ticket is for yesterday.
reaction.reading: let me HAVE a LOOK… AH, this TICK-et is for YES-ter-day.
reaction.translation: Let me check. I see: your ticket is old; it was for yesterday.

choices.translation: (Bossy) I want a new ticket now.
choices.feedback: He'll understand, but it sounds like an order. Explain the problem first, then ask politely.
choices.why: Imperatives like 'Give me…' sound bossy to strangers. Explain what happened first ('My ticket doesn't work'), then ask politely ('Could I get a new one?').

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: …Is there a problem with your ticket?
reaction.reading: …is there a PROB-lem with your TICK-et?
reaction.translation: Is something wrong with your ticket?

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: Yes, sorry. It doesn't work.
reaction.reading: YES, SOR-ry. it DOESN'T WORK.
reaction.translation: Yes. Sorry, it isn't accepted.

choices.feedback: 'Delicious' is for food! You wanted 'My ticket doesn't work'.
choices.why: 'Delicious' describes tasty food. To report a problem with something, use a verb: it doesn't work, it's broken, I've lost it.

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: Ha! I hope you didn't eat it! Let me see… Ah, it's for yesterday.
reaction.reading: HA! I HOPE you DIDN'T EAT it! let me SEE… AH, it's for YES-ter-day.
reaction.translation: Funny! Please don't eat it. Let me check… it's an old ticket from yesterday.

lines.speaker: hughes
lines.text: No problem. Where are you going?
lines.reading: no PROB-lem. WHERE are you GO-ing?
lines.translation: That's OK. What place are you travelling to?

choices.feedback: 'To + place' answers 'Where are you going?' perfectly.
choices.why: 'Where are you going?' asks about your destination. A short answer with 'to' + place is natural: 'To Camden Town.' Adding 'please' keeps it friendly.

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: Camden Town. Right you are!
reaction.reading: CAM-den TOWN. RIGHT you ARE!
reaction.translation: Camden Town. OK!

choices.translation: My home is in a different country.
choices.feedback: Nice grammar, but he asked where you're GOING, not where you're FROM.
choices.why: 'Where are you going?' (destination) and 'Where are you from?' (home country) sound similar, so listen for 'going' or 'from' at the end. This mix-up is very common!

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: Ha, welcome to London! But where are you going today?
reaction.reading: HA, WEL-come to LON-don! but WHERE are you GO-ing to-DAY?
reaction.translation: Welcome! But what place are you travelling to now?

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: Oh! To Camden Town.
reaction.reading: OH! to CAM-den TOWN.
reaction.translation: Oh, I see: Camden Town.

choices.feedback: 'Where' needs a place in the answer. 'Yes' doesn't answer a where-question.
choices.why: Questions with question words (where, what, when) can't be answered with yes or no. Only questions like 'Are you going to Camden?' take 'Yes' or 'No'.

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: Er… going where, exactly?
reaction.reading: ER… GO-ing WHERE, ex-ACT-ly?
reaction.translation: Um, to which place?

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: Oh! Camden Town!
reaction.reading: OH! CAM-den TOWN!
reaction.translation: Oh: Camden Town!

lines.speaker: hughes
lines.text: OK. You need a new ticket. You can buy one here.
lines.reading: o-KAY. you NEED a NEW TICK-et. you can BUY one HERE.
lines.translation: You must buy another ticket. You can pay me here.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Better find out the price.

choices.feedback: 'How much is it, please?' is the standard polite way to ask a price.
choices.why: 'How much' asks about price, or an amount you can't count (how much water?). 'How many' is for things you count (how many stops?). 'Please' makes it polite.

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: A single to Camden Town is two pounds eighty.
reaction.reading: a SIN-gle to CAM-den TOWN is TWO POUNDS EIGH-ty.
reaction.translation: A one-way ticket to Camden Town costs £2.80.

choices.feedback: Fine with friends, but short and blunt with staff. Try 'How much is it, please?'
choices.why: Very short questions can sound impatient in English. Full questions with 'please' sound friendlier to people you don't know.

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: …Two pounds eighty for a single.
reaction.reading: …TWO POUNDS EIGH-ty for a SIN-gle.
reaction.translation: The one-way ticket costs £2.80.

choices.feedback: 'How many' is for things you count. For a price, ask 'How much is it?'
choices.why: Use 'how many' with countable things (how many tickets, how many stops) and 'how much' for prices and uncountable things (how much money, how much time).

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: How many… tickets? Just one, I think!
reaction.reading: how MAN-y… TICK-ets? just ONE, I THINK!
reaction.translation: How many tickets? You only need one.

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: A single is two pounds eighty.
reaction.reading: a SIN-gle is TWO POUNDS EIGH-ty.
reaction.translation: A one-way ticket costs £2.80.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You pay and get a new ticket.

lines.speaker: hughes
lines.text: Take the Northern line, northbound, from platform two.
lines.reading: take the NOR-thern LINE, NORTH-bound, from PLAT-form TWO.
lines.translation: Use the train route called 'Northern', going north. It leaves from platform 2.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He said that quite fast. Which way was it again?

choices.text: Northbound, platform two. Thank you very much!
choices.reading: NORTH-bound, PLAT-form TWO. THANK you VER-y MUCH!
choices.translation: Going north, from platform 2. Thanks a lot!
choices.feedback: Repeating the key details back is a great way to check you heard correctly.
choices.why: Repeating information ('Northbound, platform two?') gives the other person a chance to correct you. English speakers do this all the time, especially with numbers and directions.

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: That's it! And mind the gap!
reaction.reading: THAT'S it! and MIND the GAP!
reaction.translation: Correct! And be careful of the space between the train and the platform!

choices.feedback: He said NORTHbound, not SOUTHbound, so you're heading the wrong way!
choices.why: '-bound' after a direction means 'travelling towards': northbound, southbound, eastbound, westbound. On the Underground, trains going both ways often leave from the same area.

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: Have a good day!
reaction.reading: have a GOOD DAY!
reaction.translation: Goodbye and enjoy your day!

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: He's already helping the next passenger. Nobody heard your mistake…

choices.text: Sorry, could you say that again, please?
choices.reading: SOR-ry, could you SAY that a-GAIN, PLEASE?
choices.translation: I didn't understand. Please repeat it.
choices.feedback: Asking someone to repeat is a real skill, and 'Could you say that again, please?' is polite and natural.
choices.why: Useful repair phrases: 'Sorry?', 'Could you say that again, please?', 'Could you speak a bit more slowly?'. Native speakers use them all the time, and asking is better than guessing.

reaction.speaker: hughes
reaction.text: Of course. The Northern line. North-bound. Platform two. Mind the gap!
reaction.reading: of COURSE. the NOR-thern LINE. NORTH-bound. PLAT-form TWO. MIND the GAP!
reaction.translation: Sure: the Northern route, going north, platform 2. Be careful getting on!

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: Northbound, platform two. Thank you!
reaction.reading: NORTH-bound, PLAT-form TWO. THANK you!
reaction.translation: Going north, platform 2. Thanks!

lines.speaker: hughes
lines.text: Your English is really good, you know!
lines.reading: your ENG-lish is REAL-ly GOOD, you KNOW!
lines.translation: You speak English very well!

lines.speaker: hughes
lines.text: Here's a map. My favourite café is right next to Camden Town station.
lines.reading: HERE'S a MAP. my FA-vour-ite CA-fé is RIGHT next to CAM-den TOWN STA-tion.
lines.translation: Take this map. The café I like best is near the station.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: He draws a little star on the map. Your first night in London just got a lot cosier.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You find platform two, squeeze onto the train and watch the stations go by.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Twenty minutes later you're standing outside your new home in Camden Town. Tired, but you made it.

lines.speaker: you
lines.text: My new flat… I made it!
lines.reading: my NEW FLAT… I MADE it!
lines.translation: This is my new apartment. I arrived!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You jump on a southbound train. The doors close behind you…

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Forty minutes later: 'This train terminates here. All change, please.' You're at the very end of the line, in the opposite direction.

lines.speaker: you
lines.text: Where… am I?
lines.reading: WHERE… AM I?
lines.translation: What is this place?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Before you can move, a student with a huge backpack taps your shoulder.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Hi! Sorry, I heard you ask him to say it again. That's so smart!
lines.reading: HI! SOR-ry, I HEARD you ASK him to SAY it a-GAIN. that's SO SMART!
lines.translation: Hello! I heard you ask him to repeat. Good idea!

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: I live in a flat in Camden Town too. Shall we go together?
lines.reading: I LIVE in a FLAT in CAM-den TOWN TOO. shall we GO to-GE-ther?
lines.translation: My apartment is in Camden Town as well. Do you want to travel with me?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Priya heard your 'I come from another country!' answer too, and couldn't stop smiling. She walks you all the way to your door. Your first friend in London.

endings.title: Smooth Traveller
endings.summary: Mr. Hughes was so impressed he marked his favourite café on your map.
endings.teachingPoint: 'Excuse me' → explain the problem → 'How much is it, please?' → repeat the details back. These four moves solve almost any travel problem.

endings.title: Made It!
endings.summary: A few bumps along the way, but you got a new ticket and reached your flat.
endings.teachingPoint: 'My ticket doesn't work' and 'How much is it, please?' will help you again and again.

endings.title: The Other End of the Line
endings.summary: You mixed up northbound and southbound and rode all the way to the end of the line.
endings.teachingPoint: Directions are easy to mix up. Repeat them back ('Northbound, platform two?') or ask: 'Could you say that again, please?'

endings.title: A Friend on the Platform
endings.summary: Your mix-up ('I come from another country!') and your polite 'Could you say that again?' caught Priya's attention. She walked you home.
endings.teachingPoint: Asking someone to repeat isn't failure. Honest questions start conversations.

phrases.text: Excuse me, my ticket doesn't work.
phrases.reading: ex-CUSE me, my TICK-et DOESN'T WORK.
phrases.translation: Sorry to bother you: the gate won't accept my ticket.
phrases.note: Get attention, then explain the problem

phrases.translation: Did you say going north, from platform 2?
phrases.note: Repeat details back to check them

phrases.text: Sorry, could you say that again, please?
phrases.reading: SOR-ry, could you SAY that a-GAIN, PLEASE?

grammar.title: Doesn't work: talking about problems
grammar.explanation: Present-tense negatives use do/does + not + verb. 'It doesn't work' is the everyday way to say something is broken or not accepted.

grammar.title: Question words decide the answer
grammar.explanation: Where needs a place, how much needs a price, when needs a time. Only questions without a question word ('Are you…?', 'Do you…?') take yes or no.
grammar.example: Where are you going? To Camden Town.

grammar.title: How much vs how many
grammar.explanation: How much = price or uncountable things (money, time, water). How many = things you can count (tickets, stops, people).
grammar.example: How many stops is it? How much is the ticket?

quiz.question: How do you politely get a stranger's attention?
quiz.explanation: 'Excuse me' is the polite way to start talking to someone you don't know.

quiz.question: 'Where are you going?' asks about…
quiz.explanation: 'Going' = where you are travelling to. 'Where are you FROM?' asks about your home country.

quiz.question: Which question asks the price?
quiz.explanation: 'How much' asks about price. 'How many' is for counting things.

survival.title: Which platform?
survival.context: You want to get to Camden Market and ask a station assistant.

steps.speaker: hughes
steps.text: For Camden? Northern line, platform three.
steps.reading: for CAM-den? NOR-thern LINE, PLAT-form THREE.
steps.translation: To go to Camden, take the Northern line from platform 3.

choices.feedback: You confirmed the platform number. Perfect.
choices.why: Repeating the number lets him correct you if you misheard.

choices.feedback: He said three, not thirteen.
choices.why: Numbers like three/thirteen and four/fourteen are easy to confuse. The -TEEN numbers have the stress at the end.

choices.feedback: He's already answering that. Listen for the platform number.
choices.why: When someone answers your question, show you understood by repeating the key detail instead of asking again.

survival.title: Delays
survival.context: You're waiting on the platform when the assistant walks over.

steps.speaker: hughes
steps.text: Sorry, the next train is delayed by fifteen minutes.
steps.reading: SOR-ry, the NEXT TRAIN is de-LAYED by fif-TEEN MIN-utes.
steps.translation: The next train is 15 minutes late. Sorry.

choices.text: OK, fifteen minutes. Thanks for letting me know.
choices.reading: o-KAY, fif-TEEN MIN-utes. THANKS for LET-ting me KNOW.
choices.translation: I understand: 15 minutes. Thanks for telling me.
choices.feedback: You confirmed the number and thanked him. Natural and polite.
choices.why: 'Thanks for letting me know' is the natural response when someone gives you news or information.

choices.feedback: He said fifTEEN (15), not FIFty (50).
choices.why: Fifteen has the stress at the END (fif-TEEN); fifty has it at the START (FIF-ty). Listen for the stress.

choices.feedback: He'll understand, but 'Thanks for letting me know' is the natural reply to news.
choices.why: To acknowledge information, say 'OK, thanks' or 'Thanks for letting me know'.

survival.title: Not enough money
survival.context: The gate beeps and won't open. You go to the assistant.

steps.speaker: hughes
steps.text: Your card doesn't have enough money on it. Do you want to top up?
steps.reading: your CARD DOESN'T have e-NOUGH MON-ey on it. do you WANT to TOP UP?
steps.translation: There isn't enough money on your card. Do you want to add more?

choices.text: Yes, please. Where can I top up?
choices.reading: YES, PLEASE. WHERE can I TOP UP?
choices.translation: Yes. Where can I add money?
choices.feedback: Exactly. You can't get through without topping up.
choices.why: 'Top up' = add money to a card or phone. 'Where can I…?' is a simple, polite question.

choices.feedback: Polite, but you can't get through the gate without topping up!
choices.why: 'I'm fine, thanks' politely declines an offer. Here the offer is the only way through, so declining doesn't solve your problem.

choices.feedback: You top up a CARD, not a person: 'Can I top up my card?'
choices.why: Phrasal verbs keep their object: top up a card, top up a phone. 'Top me' doesn't mean anything!

survival.title: Urgent!
survival.context: You really need the toilet. You find the assistant.

choices.text: Yes, please. Where are the toilets?
choices.reading: YES, PLEASE. WHERE are the TOI-lets?
choices.translation: Yes. Where can I find the toilets?
choices.feedback: Clear and polite. ('Toilets' is normal in the UK.)
choices.why: 'Where is/are…?' is the go-to pattern for places. In the UK people say 'toilets' or 'loo'; in the US 'restroom'.

choices.feedback: 'I lost…' means you can't find something you own. Ask 'Where are the toilets?'
choices.why: Don't reuse a phrase just because it worked before. Ask for a place with 'Where is/are…?'.

choices.feedback: One word works in an emergency, but the full question is easy and polite.
choices.why: Single words get understood, but 'Excuse me, where are the toilets?' sounds much more natural.

survival.title: Lost property
survival.context: You left something on the train and go to the station office.

choices.feedback: You named what you lost. That's exactly what he needs.
choices.why: 'What' asks for a thing, so answer with the object: 'I lost my wallet / phone / bag'.

choices.feedback: 'What' needs a thing in the answer, not 'yes'.
choices.why: Questions with a question word (what, where, when) can't be answered with yes or no.

choices.text: Can you give me a wallet?
choices.reading: can you GIVE me a WAL-let?
choices.feedback: That asks for a new wallet! He needs to know what you lost.
choices.why: Report what happened (past tense: 'I lost my wallet') before asking for help.

survival.title: Which exit?
survival.context: You need the exit for the market. You ask the assistant.

steps.speaker: hughes
steps.text: Exit A is on the left, Exit B is on the right. Exit A goes to the market.
steps.reading: EX-it A is on the LEFT, EX-it B is on the RIGHT. EX-it A goes to the MAR-ket.
steps.translation: Go left for exit A, which leads to the market. Exit B is on the right.

choices.text: Exit A, on the left. Thank you!
choices.reading: EX-it A, on the LEFT. THANK you!
choices.translation: Exit A, to the left. Thanks!
choices.feedback: You picked out the detail you needed and confirmed it.
choices.why: When someone gives you two options, repeat the one you need: 'Exit A, on the left.'

choices.text: Exit B, on the left. Thanks!
choices.reading: EX-it B, on the LEFT. THANKS!
choices.translation: Exit B, to the left. Thanks!
choices.feedback: Exit B is on the RIGHT, and it doesn't go to the market.
choices.why: Listen for the letter AND the direction. Repeating them back helps you catch mistakes.

choices.text: Is it a left or a right?
choices.reading: is it a LEFT or a RIGHT?
choices.translation: (Mistake) Is it a left or a right?
choices.feedback: He already told you. And we say 'on the left/right' (no 'a').
choices.why: Directions: 'on the left', 'on the right', 'turn left', 'go straight on'.

episodes.title: Coffee Rush
episodes.goal: Order breakfast at a busy café before class.
episodes.synopsis: Day 3. The café is packed, the barista talks fast, and class starts in twenty minutes.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Day 3. Class starts in twenty minutes, and you really need coffee.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The café is packed. When it's finally your turn, the barista smiles.

lines.speaker: leo
lines.text: Hiya! Sorry about the queue. What can I get you?
lines.reading: HI-ya! SOR-ry a-BOUT the QUEUE. WHAT can I GET you?
lines.translation: Hi! Sorry you had to wait. What would you like?

choices.text: Hi! Could I have a latte, please?
choices.reading: HI! could I HAVE a LAT-te, PLEASE?
choices.translation: Hello! I'd like a milky coffee, please.
choices.feedback: 'Could I have…, please?' is a polite, natural way to order.
choices.why: English orders usually use 'Could I have…?', 'Can I get…?' or 'I'd like…', plus 'please'. 'Could' sounds a little more polite than 'can'.

reaction.speaker: leo
reaction.text: Lovely. One latte coming up!
reaction.reading: LOVE-ly. ONE LAT-te COM-ing UP!
reaction.translation: Great. I'll make one latte now!

choices.feedback: Clear, but 'I want' can sound demanding. Try 'Could I have…?' or 'I'd like…'.
choices.why: 'I want' is very direct. In shops and cafés, English speakers soften it: 'I'd like a latte, please' or 'Could I have a latte?'. Same meaning, much friendlier.

reaction.speaker: leo
reaction.text: …Sure. One latte.
reaction.reading: …SURE. ONE LAT-te.
reaction.translation: OK. One latte.

choices.feedback: That sounds like an order, and it needs 'a': 'a latte'. Try 'Could I have a latte, please?'
choices.why: Countable nouns like 'latte' need 'a' or 'the' (a latte, the latte). And imperatives like 'Give me…' sound rude when ordering.

reaction.speaker: leo
reaction.text: Er… one latte. Right.
reaction.reading: ER… ONE LAT-te. RIGHT.
reaction.translation: Um, OK, one latte.

lines.speaker: leo
lines.text: Is that to have in or take away?
lines.reading: is THAT to have IN or take a-WAY?
lines.translation: Will you drink it here in the café, or take it with you?

choices.text: Take away, please. I'm in a rush!
choices.reading: take a-WAY, PLEASE. I'm IN a RUSH!
choices.translation: I'll take it with me. I'm in a hurry.
choices.feedback: 'Take away' means you'll leave with it. Perfect when you're in a hurry.
choices.why: In the UK: 'to have in' / 'eat in' = stay in the café; 'take away' = take it with you. In the US you'll hear 'For here or to go?'. Same question!

reaction.speaker: leo
reaction.text: Takeaway it is!
reaction.reading: TAKE-a-way it IS!
reaction.translation: OK, a drink to take with you!

choices.feedback: It's an either/or question, so choose one: 'To have in' or 'Take away'.
choices.why: Questions with 'or' ask you to choose. 'Yes, please' doesn't tell the barista which one you want.

reaction.speaker: leo
reaction.text: Er… which one? In, or take away?
reaction.reading: ER… WHICH one? IN, or take a-WAY?
reaction.translation: Which do you want: here, or to take with you?

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: Oh! Take away, please.
reaction.reading: OH! take a-WAY, PLEASE.
reaction.translation: Oh, I'll take it with me, please.

choices.feedback: 'To have in' means drinking it in the café. It's not about owning something!
choices.why: 'Have' has many meanings: 'have a coffee' = drink one; 'to have in' = drink it here. Listen to the whole phrase, not just one word.

reaction.speaker: leo
reaction.text: No, I mean… having it in? Drinking it here?
reaction.reading: NO, I MEAN… HAV-ing it IN? DRINK-ing it HERE?
reaction.translation: I'm asking if you'll drink it in the café.

reaction.speaker: narrator
reaction.text: Before you can answer, he pours your latte into a big china mug.

lines.speaker: leo
lines.text: Anything else? We've got fresh croissants today.
lines.reading: AN-y-thing ELSE? we've got FRESH CROIS-sants to-DAY.
lines.translation: Do you want something more? We have new croissants.

choices.feedback: 'That's all, thanks' politely tells him you've finished ordering.
choices.why: 'Anything else?' asks if you want more. Answer 'No, that's all, thanks' or 'Yes, could I also have…?'.

reaction.speaker: leo
reaction.text: Lovely. That's three pounds forty, please.
reaction.reading: LOVE-ly. THAT'S THREE POUNDS FOR-ty, PLEASE.
reaction.translation: OK. It costs £3.40.

choices.feedback: Understandable, but a bit abrupt. 'No, that's all, thanks' is friendlier.
choices.why: One-word answers can sound cold in English. Adding 'thanks', or making a full sentence ('No, that's all, thanks'), sounds warmer.

reaction.speaker: leo
reaction.text: …Right. Three pounds forty, please.
reaction.reading: …RIGHT. THREE POUNDS FOR-ty, PLEASE.
reaction.translation: OK. It costs £3.40.

choices.feedback: 'Else' means 'other' or 'more'. You can't BE 'else'! Say 'No, that's all' or 'Yes, a croissant, please'.
choices.why: 'Else' follows words like anything, something, nothing and someone: 'anything else?', 'something else', 'nobody else'. It never comes after 'I'm'.

reaction.speaker: leo
reaction.text: You're… else? Ha! I think you mean 'that's all'. Three pounds forty, please.
reaction.reading: you're… ELSE? HA! I THINK you mean THAT'S ALL. THREE POUNDS FOR-ty, PLEASE.
reaction.translation: You are 'else'? Funny! You mean you don't want more. It costs £3.40.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You check your pocket… you only have three pounds! Then you notice your flatmate Priya, a few people behind you.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Oh, hi! Fancy seeing you in the queue! Everything OK?
lines.reading: OH, HI! FAN-cy SEE-ing you in the QUEUE! EV-ery-thing o-KAY?
lines.translation: Hi! What a surprise to see you here! Is everything fine?

choices.text: Hi Priya! Could you lend me 50p? I'm a bit short.
choices.reading: HI PRI-ya! could you LEND me fif-ty PEE? I'm a BIT SHORT.
choices.translation: Hi! Can you give me 50 pence for a while? I don't have enough money.
choices.feedback: 'Lend me' is right: Priya gives, you receive. 'I'm a bit short' means you don't have enough money.
choices.why: 'Lend' = give something for a while; 'borrow' = take something for a while. So: 'Can you lend me 50p?' or 'Can I borrow 50p?', but never 'Can you borrow me…?'.

reaction.speaker: priya
reaction.text: Of course! Here you go.
reaction.reading: of COURSE! HERE you GO.
reaction.translation: Sure! Take it.

choices.text: Hi Priya! Can you borrow me 50p?
choices.reading: HI PRI-ya! can you BOR-row me fif-ty PEE?
choices.feedback: A very common mistake! 'Borrow' is what YOU do. Say 'Can you lend me…?' or 'Can I borrow…?'.
choices.why: 'Borrow' means take for a while; 'lend' means give for a while. The person who gives lends; the person who receives borrows.

reaction.speaker: priya
reaction.text: Ha, you mean 'lend'! Sure, you can borrow 50p.
reaction.reading: HA, you MEAN LEND! SURE, you can BOR-row fif-ty PEE.
reaction.translation: You mean 'lend'. Yes, you can have 50p for now.

choices.feedback: That sounds like a robbery! Ask politely: 'Could you lend me 50p?'
choices.why: Requests for help need softening in English: 'Could you lend me…?', 'Would you mind…?'. Bare imperatives like 'Give me money!' sound aggressive.

reaction.speaker: priya
reaction.text: Whoa! …Oh, you're a bit short? Here.
reaction.reading: WHOA! …OH, you're a BIT SHORT? HERE.
reaction.translation: Wow! Oh, you don't have enough money? Take this.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You pay, grab your latte and step aside with Priya.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: So, how's it going? Settling in OK?
lines.reading: SO, HOW'S it GO-ing? SET-tling IN o-KAY?
lines.translation: How are you? Are you getting used to life here?

choices.text: Yeah, not bad! Still a bit jet-lagged, though. You?
choices.reading: YEAH, not BAD! STILL a bit JET-lagged, though. YOU?
choices.translation: I'm OK! I'm still tired from the flight. And you?
choices.feedback: A casual reply, then 'You?' to return the question. Perfect with a friend.
choices.why: 'How's it going?' is casual. Natural answers: 'Not bad!', 'Pretty good, thanks!'. Then ask back: 'You?' or 'How about you?'

reaction.speaker: priya
reaction.text: Same here! Hey, shall we walk to class together?
reaction.reading: SAME HERE! HEY, shall we WALK to CLASS to-GE-ther?
reaction.translation: Me too! Do you want to walk to class with me?

choices.text: I am fine, thank you. And you?
choices.reading: I am FINE, THANK you. and YOU?
choices.translation: I am well. How are you?
choices.feedback: Correct, but it sounds like a textbook. With friends, try 'Not bad! You?'
choices.why: 'I'm fine, thank you, and you?' is taught everywhere, but in casual English it can sound stiff. Mix it up: 'Pretty good!', 'Not bad, thanks!'

reaction.speaker: priya
reaction.text: Ha, so formal! I'm good, thanks.
reaction.reading: HA, so FOR-mal! I'm GOOD, THANKS.
reaction.translation: That's very formal! I'm well, thank you.

choices.feedback: 'How's it going?' is a greeting, not a question about where something is going!
choices.why: Some English greetings aren't literal: 'How's it going?', 'What's up?' and 'How are you doing?' all just mean 'How are you?'.

reaction.speaker: priya
reaction.text: Ha… what's going to the station? I meant, how are YOU?
reaction.reading: HA… WHAT'S going to the STA-tion? I MEANT, how are YOU?
reaction.translation: What is going where? I was asking how you are!

lines.speaker: leo
lines.text: Here, a croissant on the house! Anything else, just ask.
lines.reading: HERE, a CROIS-sant on the HOUSE! AN-y-thing ELSE, just ASK.
lines.translation: Take this croissant for free! If you want more, tell me.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Lucky you! Could I have a bite? Come on, let's walk to class together.
lines.reading: LUCK-y YOU! could I HAVE a BITE? come ON, let's WALK to CLASS to-GE-ther.
lines.translation: You're lucky! Can I taste it? Let's go to class with each other.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You walk to class sharing a free croissant. Not bad for day three.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You hurry down the street, hot coffee in hand.

lines.speaker: you
lines.text: One latte to take away… and I'm not late!
lines.reading: ONE LAT-te to take a-WAY… and I'm NOT LATE!
lines.translation: I have my coffee with me, and I'm on time!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Leo hands you a huge china mug. It's for drinking IN the café, and class starts in five minutes.

lines.speaker: you
lines.text: Oh no… I should have said 'take away'!
lines.reading: OH NO… I SHOULD have SAID take a-WAY!
lines.translation: Oh no, I needed to ask to take it with me!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: You gulp it down, burn your tongue and run. Lesson learned: listen for 'in or take away?'

lines.speaker: leo
lines.text: Morning, Else! How's it going? What can I get you… else?
lines.reading: MOR-ning, ELSE! HOW'S it GO-ing? WHAT can I GET you… ELSE?
lines.translation: Good morning, 'Else'! How are you? What would you like?

lines.speaker: leo
lines.text: Need to borrow anything from Priya again?
lines.reading: NEED to BOR-row AN-y-thing from PRI-ya a-GAIN?
lines.translation: Do you need to take money from Priya again?

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The customer who wanted to BE 'else' and asked Priya to 'borrow' them money? Leo tells everyone. By Friday the whole café calls you 'Else'.

endings.title: Coffee Champion
endings.summary: Every exchange went smoothly, so Leo gave you a free croissant and Priya walked you to class.
endings.teachingPoint: Polite ordering in three steps: 'Could I have…, please?' → 'Take away, please' → 'No, that's all, thanks.'

endings.title: Caffeine Secured
endings.summary: A couple of wobbles, but you got your latte to take away and made it to class.
endings.teachingPoint: Listen for 'or' questions ('in or take away?') and choose one option.

endings.title: The Mug Mix-Up
endings.summary: You misunderstood 'to have in', got your latte in a mug, and had to gulp it down before class.
endings.teachingPoint: 'To have in' = drink it here; 'take away' = take it with you. In the US: 'for here or to go?'

endings.title: Known as 'Else'
endings.summary: Your two best mistakes made you famous at the café: the staff now call you 'Else'.
endings.teachingPoint: 'Else' only follows words like anything, something and nothing. And remember: you BORROW from someone; they LEND to you.

phrases.text: Could I have a latte, please?
phrases.reading: could I HAVE a LAT-te, PLEASE?

phrases.note: Answering 'to have in or take away?'

phrases.reading: could you LEND me fif-ty PEE?
phrases.translation: Can you give me 50 pence for a while?

grammar.title: Polite requests: Could I have…?
grammar.explanation: 'Could I have…?', 'Can I get…?' and 'I'd like…' are the natural ways to order. 'I want…' and 'Give me…' sound too direct.
grammar.example: Could I have a cup of tea, please?
grammar.exampleTranslation: A polite way to order tea.

grammar.title: Lend vs borrow
grammar.explanation: Lend = give for a while (Can you lend me…?). Borrow = take for a while (Can I borrow…?). The giver lends; the receiver borrows.
grammar.example: Can I borrow your pen? / Can you lend me your pen?
grammar.exampleTranslation: Both ask to use the pen for a while.

grammar.title: Either/or questions
grammar.explanation: A question with 'or' asks you to choose. Answer with one of the options, not 'yes'.

quiz.question: Which order sounds most natural?
options: Could I have a latte, please?
quiz.explanation: 'Could I have…, please?' is polite and natural. 'Latte' also needs 'a'.

quiz.question: The barista asks 'To have in or take away?' You're in a rush. You say:
quiz.explanation: It's an either/or question. 'Take away' means you'll take it with you.

quiz.question: Which sentence is correct?
quiz.explanation: The giver LENDS: 'Could you lend me…?' Or: 'Could I borrow…?'

survival.title: Receipt?
survival.context: You've just paid at the café.

steps.speaker: leo
steps.translation: Do you want the paper that shows what you paid?

choices.feedback: A soft, friendly 'no thanks'.
choices.why: 'I'm fine, thanks' or 'No, thanks' politely declines an offer.

choices.feedback: 'Want' needs an object: 'Yes, please' or 'Yes, I'd like it, thanks'.
choices.why: In English, 'want' and 'like' need something after them: 'I want it', 'I'd like one'.

choices.feedback: 'Delicious' is for food, and it doesn't answer the question.
choices.why: Answer offers with 'Yes, please' or 'No, thanks'.

survival.title: What size?
survival.context: You're ordering a tea at another café.

choices.feedback: You chose one option. Perfect.
choices.why: Questions with 'or' need one of the options as the answer.

choices.feedback: It's a choice question. Pick one size.
choices.why: 'Yes' doesn't choose. Say the option: 'Small, please.'

choices.feedback: Use the words he gave you and add 'please': 'Large, please.'
choices.why: Echoing the options ('Large, please') is the easiest natural answer.

survival.title: Milk or sugar?
survival.context: The barista hands you a black coffee.

steps.speaker: leo
steps.text: Would you like any milk or sugar?
steps.reading: would you LIKE any MILK or SU-gar?
steps.translation: Do you want milk or sugar in it?

choices.translation: A small amount of milk, please.
choices.feedback: Clear and polite.
choices.why: 'A little' works with uncountable things like milk and sugar.

choices.feedback: 'Like' needs an object: 'Yes, I'd like some milk.'
choices.why: 'Would like' must be followed by something: 'I'd like some milk', 'I'd like to sit'.

choices.feedback: You said you ARE milk! Try 'No, thanks' or 'Just milk, please'.
choices.why: Be careful with 'I'm…': it describes you, not what you want.

steps.speaker: leo
steps.translation: Will you pay with a card or with money?

choices.feedback: One option + please. Perfect.
choices.why: Short answers are natural for choice questions: 'Card, please.'

choices.feedback: It's either/or, so pick one.
choices.why: 'Yes' doesn't answer 'card or cash?'. Choose: 'Cash, please.'

choices.feedback: You just told him you lost your card!
choices.why: Make sure the phrase matches the situation.

steps.speaker: leo
steps.translation: Do you want it hot or cold with ice?

choices.text: Iced, please. It's so warm today!
choices.reading: ICED, PLEASE. it's SO WARM to-DAY!
choices.translation: With ice, please. It's hot today!
choices.feedback: Clear choice plus friendly small talk.
choices.why: Adding a short comment ('It's so warm today!') makes service chats friendlier.

choices.feedback: 'I'm hot' describes YOU (and can even mean attractive!). Say 'Iced, please.'
choices.why: 'I'm hot / I'm cold' describe how your body feels; they don't order a drink.

choices.feedback: That doesn't make sense. Choose one: 'Hot, please' or 'Iced, please'.
choices.why: For either/or questions, say one option.

survival.title: Weekend plans
survival.context: Priya catches you outside the café.

steps.speaker: priya
steps.text: Fancy going to the cinema on Saturday?
steps.reading: FAN-cy GO-ing to the CIN-e-ma on SAT-ur-day?
steps.translation: Do you want to go to the cinema on Saturday?

choices.feedback: Enthusiastic and natural with a friend.
choices.why: 'Fancy…?' is British English for 'Do you want to…?'. Answer warmly and ask for details.

choices.feedback: Here 'fancy' is a verb meaning 'want to'. 'I'm fancy' means you're elegant!
choices.why: 'Fancy + -ing?' = 'Do you want to…?'. Answer 'Yes!' or 'I'd love to!'.

choices.feedback: Clear, but very blunt. Softer: 'Sorry, I can't this weekend.'
choices.why: Soften refusals with 'Sorry', 'I'd love to, but…' or 'Maybe next time?'.

episodes.title: The Bookshop Interview
episodes.goal: Get a part-time job at Chapter One bookshop.
episodes.synopsis: Day 6. Your savings are melting. Priya got you an interview, so now switch from casual chat with her to polite English with the manager.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Day 6. Your savings are disappearing faster than your coffee. Time for a part-time job.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Priya works at Chapter One, a little bookshop near your flat, and she's set up an interview for you.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: You made it! The manager's just finishing a call. Nervous?
lines.reading: you MADE it! the MAN-a-ger's just FIN-ish-ing a CALL. NER-vous?
lines.translation: You came! The boss is almost free. Are you worried?

choices.text: A bit, yeah. But I'm excited!
choices.reading: a BIT, YEAH. but I'm ex-CI-ted!
choices.translation: A little. But I'm also happy about it!
choices.feedback: Casual 'A bit, yeah' matches Priya, and 'excited' is exactly right.
choices.why: -ED adjectives describe how you feel (I'm excited, I'm bored, I'm interested). -ING adjectives describe what causes the feeling (an exciting job, a boring film).

reaction.speaker: priya
reaction.text: That's the spirit! Don't worry, the manager is lovely.
reaction.reading: THAT'S the SPI-rit! DON'T WOR-ry, the MAN-a-ger is LOVE-ly.
reaction.translation: Great attitude! Relax, the boss is very nice.

choices.translation: (Mistake) Yes, I make other people very excited.
choices.feedback: 'I'm exciting' means you make OTHER people excited! You mean 'I'm excited'.
choices.why: -ED = how you feel; -ING = what causes the feeling. 'I'm exciting' describes you as a thrilling person! The same goes for bored/boring and interested/interesting.

reaction.speaker: priya
reaction.text: Ha! Well, you ARE exciting… but I think you mean 'excited'!
reaction.reading: HA! WELL, you ARE ex-CI-ting… but I THINK you mean ex-CI-ted!
reaction.translation: Funny! You mean you FEEL excited.

choices.text: Indeed, I am rather apprehensive at present.
choices.reading: in-DEED, I am RA-ther ap-pre-HEN-sive at PRES-ent.
choices.translation: (Very formal) Yes, I am feeling quite worried right now.
choices.feedback: Very formal for a chat with a friend. It sounds like a robot butler! Try 'A bit, yeah!'
choices.why: English has registers too. With friends, use short, relaxed sentences. Words like 'indeed', 'rather' and 'at present' belong in formal writing or speeches.

reaction.speaker: priya
reaction.text: Ha, 'apprehensive'! Save the big words for the interview!
reaction.reading: HA, ap-pre-HEN-sive! SAVE the BIG WORDS for the IN-ter-view!
reaction.translation: Such a formal word! Use those in the interview, not with me.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: A woman with reading glasses walks over. Priya slips back behind the counter.

lines.speaker: clarke
lines.text: Hello, you must be here for the interview. I'm Helen Clarke, the manager. Please, have a seat.
lines.reading: hel-LO, you MUST be HERE for the IN-ter-view. I'm HE-len CLARKE, the MAN-a-ger. PLEASE, have a SEAT.
lines.translation: Hi, you've come for the job meeting. I'm Helen Clarke, the boss. Please sit down.

choices.text: Nice to meet you, Ms. Clarke. Thank you for seeing me.
choices.reading: NICE to MEET you, ms CLARKE. THANK you for SEE-ing me.
choices.translation: Hello, Ms. Clarke. Thank you for your time.
choices.feedback: Polite, warm and professional: a perfect interview opening.
choices.why: Use a title + surname (Ms. Clarke) until you're invited to use a first name. 'Thank you for seeing me' is a classic, polite interview opener.

reaction.speaker: clarke
reaction.text: Nice to meet you too. Please, call me Helen.
reaction.reading: NICE to MEET you TOO. PLEASE, call me HE-len.
reaction.translation: I'm happy to meet you. You can use my first name.

choices.translation: (Very casual) Hi Helen! How are things?
choices.feedback: Too casual for a first meeting with a manager. You brought Priya's tone into the interview.
choices.why: 'Hiya' and 'What's up?' are for friends. In interviews, start formally (Ms. Clarke) and let the interviewer invite you to be more relaxed.

reaction.speaker: clarke
reaction.text: …Hello. Not much. Please, sit down.
reaction.reading: …hel-LO. NOT MUCH. PLEASE, sit DOWN.
reaction.translation: Um, hi. Nothing special. Please sit.

choices.text: Nice to meet you, Ms. Helen.
choices.reading: NICE to MEET you, ms HE-len.
choices.feedback: Close! Titles go with the surname: Ms. Clarke, not Ms. Helen.
choices.why: In English, Mr/Ms/Mrs/Dr goes with the SURNAME: Ms. Clarke, Dr. Patel. 'Ms. + first name' sounds odd. If you're not sure about Mrs/Miss, 'Ms.' is the safe choice.

reaction.speaker: clarke
reaction.text: Ha, just 'Helen' is fine!
reaction.reading: HA, just HE-len is FINE!
reaction.translation: Funny! You can just call me Helen.

lines.speaker: clarke
lines.text: So, why would you like to work at Chapter One?
lines.reading: SO, WHY would you LIKE to WORK at CHAP-ter ONE?
lines.translation: Why do you want this job?

choices.text: I love books, and I'd like to improve my English by talking to customers.
choices.reading: I LOVE BOOKS, and I'd LIKE to im-PROVE my ENG-lish by TALK-ing to CUS-to-mers.
choices.translation: Books are my passion, and I want to practise English with shoppers.
choices.feedback: Motivation linked to the job and to growth: exactly what interviewers hope to hear.
choices.why: Good answers connect you to the job: the product (books), the customers, or what you'll learn. 'I'd like to…' is a polite way to talk about wishes.

reaction.speaker: clarke
reaction.text: Lovely. Our customers do love a chat, so that's perfect.
reaction.reading: LOVE-ly. our CUS-to-mers DO love a CHAT, so THAT'S PER-fect.
reaction.translation: Great. The people who shop here enjoy talking, so that works well.

choices.feedback: Honest and grammatical, but leading with money can sound blunt in an interview.
choices.why: Pay matters! But in interviews, talk about the work first. You can ask about pay later, or when they make you an offer.

reaction.speaker: clarke
reaction.text: …Well, that's honest. The pay is eleven pounds fifty an hour.
reaction.reading: …WELL, that's HON-est. the PAY is e-LEV-en POUNDS FIF-ty an HOUR.
reaction.translation: You're very direct. We pay £11.50 an hour.

choices.translation: (Casual slang) I really love books, friend!
choices.feedback: Enthusiastic! But 'mate' is too casual for an interview.
choices.why: 'Mate' is friendly British slang for friends and coworkers, not for a manager you've just met. Save it for when you know people well.

reaction.speaker: clarke
reaction.text: 'Mate'! Ha. Well, I'm glad you like books.
reaction.reading: MATE! HA. WELL, I'm GLAD you like BOOKS.
reaction.translation: You called me 'mate'! Funny. I'm happy you love books.

lines.speaker: clarke
lines.text: And when would you be able to start?
lines.reading: and WHEN would you be A-ble to START?
lines.translation: From what date can you begin working?

choices.feedback: 'When… start' asks for a date, and 'next Monday' answers it precisely.
choices.why: 'Would you be able to…?' is a polite way of saying 'Can you…?'. Answer with a time: 'next Monday', 'from the 15th', 'right away'.

reaction.speaker: clarke
reaction.text: Next Monday. That would really help us.
reaction.reading: NEXT MON-day. that would REAL-ly HELP us.
reaction.translation: Next Monday is very useful for us.

choices.translation: I'm free to work seven days a week!
choices.feedback: Keen! But she asked WHEN you can start, not how often you can work.
choices.why: Listen for the question word: 'when' = a time or date; 'how often' = frequency; 'how long' = duration.

reaction.speaker: clarke
reaction.text: Every day…? And when could you START?
reaction.reading: EV-ery DAY…? and WHEN could you START?
reaction.translation: Every day? But from which date can you begin?

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: Oh, sorry! From next Monday.
reaction.reading: OH, SOR-ry! from NEXT MON-day.
reaction.translation: Oh! From next Monday.

choices.feedback: That's the past tense, so it sounds like you already started! Say 'I could start next Monday'.
choices.why: 'Would you be able to start?' is about the future. Use 'can/could + start' with a future time (next week, on Monday).

reaction.speaker: clarke
reaction.text: …You've already started? Without telling me?
reaction.reading: …YOU'VE al-READ-y START-ed? with-OUT TELL-ing me?
reaction.translation: You began already? I didn't know!

reaction.speaker: you
reaction.text: No, no! I could start next Monday!
reaction.reading: NO, NO! I could START next MON-day!
reaction.translation: No! I can begin next Monday!

lines.speaker: clarke
lines.text: Finally, do you have any questions for me?
lines.reading: FI-nal-ly, do you HAVE any QUES-tions for ME?
lines.translation: Last thing: is there anything you want to ask me?

choices.text: Yes. Could you tell me a bit about the training?
choices.reading: YES. could you TELL me a BIT a-BOUT the TRAIN-ing?
choices.translation: Yes. Please explain how you teach new staff.
choices.feedback: An indirect question ('Could you tell me…?') is polite, and asking about training shows you're serious.
choices.why: Indirect questions like 'Could you tell me…?' or 'I was wondering if…' soften requests. They're very common in professional English.

reaction.speaker: clarke
reaction.text: Of course! Your first shift is training with Priya.
reaction.reading: of COURSE! your FIRST SHIFT is TRAIN-ing with PRI-ya.
reaction.translation: Sure! On your first work day, Priya will teach you.

choices.feedback: Polite enough, but you miss a chance to show interest. Have one question ready.
choices.why: Interviewers often see 'Do you have any questions?' as a chance to show motivation. Prepare one: the training, the team, or a typical day.

reaction.speaker: clarke
reaction.text: Right. Well, if you think of something, could you tell me later?
reaction.reading: RIGHT. WELL, if you THINK of SOME-thing, could you TELL me LA-ter?
reaction.translation: I see. If you have a question later, please tell me.

choices.translation: Do workers get books without paying?
choices.feedback: Fun question! Staff discounts are a real perk. But it's a bold first question.
choices.why: Asking about perks is normal, usually after you get an offer. As your only question, it can sound like you're mainly there for the freebies!

reaction.speaker: clarke
reaction.text: Ha! Not free, but staff get thirty percent off.
reaction.reading: HA! NOT FREE, but STAFF get THIR-ty per-CENT OFF.
reaction.translation: Funny! You don't get them free, but you pay 30% less.

lines.speaker: clarke
lines.text: Thank you for coming in today. Your English is excellent.
lines.reading: THANK you for COM-ing IN to-DAY. your ENG-lish is EX-cel-lent.
lines.translation: Thanks for visiting. You speak English very well.

lines.speaker: clarke
lines.text: Could you start with a Saturday shift next week?
lines.reading: could you START with a SAT-ur-day SHIFT next WEEK?
lines.translation: Can you begin with a Saturday work day next week?

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Yes! We'll be working together!
lines.reading: YES! we'll be WORK-ing to-GE-ther!
lines.translation: Great! We'll work with each other!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Two days later, your phone buzzes. It's Chapter One.

lines.speaker: clarke
lines.text: Hello, it's Helen from Chapter One. We'd love you to start next week!
lines.reading: hel-LO, it's HE-len from CHAP-ter ONE. we'd LOVE you to START next WEEK!
lines.translation: Hi, this is Helen from the bookshop. We want you to begin work next week!

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Ms. Clarke thanks you politely… a little too politely. You know what that means.

lines.speaker: priya
lines.text: Hey, don't worry! Interviews make everyone nervous. Let's practise together.
lines.reading: HEY, DON'T WOR-ry! IN-ter-views make EV-ery-one NER-vous. let's PRAC-tise to-GE-ther.
lines.translation: Relax! Everyone gets worried in job interviews. Let's practise with each other.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Over hot chocolate, Priya plays the manager and you practise: 'Nice to meet you, Ms. Clarke…'. Next time, you'll be ready.

lines.speaker: clarke
lines.text: Honestly? I said exactly the same thing at my first interview. 'Books are my life!'
lines.reading: HON-est-ly? I SAID ex-ACT-ly the SAME THING at my FIRST IN-ter-view. BOOKS are my LIFE!
lines.translation: To be honest, I said the same words when I applied for my first job.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Your too-casual passion struck a chord. Helen asks you to run the shop's new book club, and you spend the afternoon talking about your favourite novels.

endings.title: Hired on the Spot
endings.summary: Ms. Clarke hired you on the spot, and you'll be working shifts with Priya.
endings.teachingPoint: Switching registers is the real skill: casual with Priya ('A bit, yeah!'), polite with the manager ('Nice to meet you, Ms. Clarke').

endings.title: The Callback
endings.summary: A few wobbles, but your effort showed: the shop called two days later to offer you the job.
endings.teachingPoint: In interviews, listen for the question word (when, why, what) and answer exactly that.

endings.title: Interview Practice Club
endings.summary: The interview didn't land, but Priya turned it into a hot-chocolate practice session.
endings.teachingPoint: Casual ('Hiya!'), neutral ('Hello') and formal ('Nice to meet you, Ms. Clarke') are different gears. Interviews need the polite ones.

endings.title: Fellow Bookworm
endings.summary: Your casual love of books (and your cheeky question about free books) turned a stiff interview into a book chat. You're running the new book club!
endings.teachingPoint: 'Mate' and 'free books?' aren't textbook interview English, but real enthusiasm opens doors. Learn the rules first, then learn when to bend them.

phrases.text: Nice to meet you, Ms. Clarke. Thank you for seeing me.
phrases.reading: NICE to MEET you, ms CLARKE. THANK you for SEE-ing me.

phrases.text: Could you tell me a bit about the training?
phrases.reading: could you TELL me a BIT a-BOUT the TRAIN-ing?

phrases.text: A bit, yeah. But I'm excited!
phrases.reading: a BIT, YEAH. but I'm ex-CI-ted!
phrases.translation: A little nervous, but happy too!

grammar.title: -ed vs -ing adjectives
grammar.explanation: -ED describes how you feel (excited, bored, interested). -ING describes what causes the feeling (exciting, boring, interesting).
grammar.example: I'm excited. The job is exciting.

grammar.title: Titles: Mr / Ms + surname
grammar.explanation: Formal English uses a title with the SURNAME: Ms. Clarke, Mr. Hughes, Dr. Patel. Use first names only when invited.
grammar.example: Nice to meet you, Ms. Clarke.

grammar.title: Indirect questions
grammar.explanation: 'Could you tell me…?', 'Do you know…?' and 'I was wondering if…' make questions softer and more polite. The word order after them is like a statement.
grammar.example: Could you tell me where the station is?

quiz.question: Before an interview you feel happy and full of energy. You say:
quiz.explanation: -ED describes how you feel. 'I'm exciting' means you excite other people!

quiz.question: How do you address Helen Clarke in a formal first meeting?
quiz.explanation: Title + surname is the polite default until you're invited to use a first name.

quiz.question: 'When would you be able to start?' asks about…
quiz.explanation: 'When' asks for a time or date.

survival.title: First shift
survival.context: It's your first day at Chapter One.

steps.speaker: clarke
steps.text: Welcome! Ready for your first shift?
steps.reading: WEL-come! READ-y for your FIRST SHIFT?
steps.translation: Hello! Are you prepared for your first work day?

choices.text: Yes, I'm really looking forward to it!
choices.reading: YES, I'm REAL-ly LOOK-ing FOR-ward to it!
choices.translation: Yes, I'm happy and excited about it!
choices.feedback: Warm, positive and natural.
choices.why: 'Look forward to' + noun or -ing: 'I'm looking forward to it / to working here'.

choices.text: Yes, I'm looking forward to work here.
choices.reading: YES, I'm LOOK-ing FOR-ward to WORK HERE.
choices.translation: (Small mistake) Yes, I look forward to work here.
choices.feedback: Close! After 'looking forward to', use -ing: 'to working here'.
choices.why: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so the verb takes -ing: looking forward to meeting you.

choices.translation: Yes, I am a dull person.
choices.feedback: 'I'm boring' means you're a dull person! And it's not a great thing to say on day one.
choices.why: -ING describes what causes a feeling. To describe your feeling, use -ED: 'I'm excited / I'm nervous'.

survival.title: End of shift
survival.context: Your shift is over and you're heading home.

steps.speaker: clarke
steps.text: Thanks for today, see you tomorrow!
steps.reading: THANKS for to-DAY, SEE you to-MOR-row!
steps.translation: Thank you for working today. See you tomorrow!

choices.feedback: Friendly and natural, and she invited you to call her Helen.
choices.why: Return the greeting: 'See you tomorrow!' / 'Have a good evening!'

choices.translation: I will never see you again!
choices.feedback: 'Forever' sounds like you're quitting!
choices.why: Everyday goodbyes at work: 'See you tomorrow!', 'Bye, have a good one!'

choices.feedback: Honest! But she said goodbye, so say goodbye back.
choices.why: Respond to 'See you tomorrow' with a goodbye, not a description of how you feel.

survival.title: A customer
survival.context: Leo from the café comes in as a customer.

steps.speaker: leo
steps.text: Excuse me, do you have any books about coffee?
steps.reading: ex-CUSE me, do you HAVE any BOOKS a-BOUT COF-fee?
steps.translation: Hello, are there any books about coffee here?

choices.text: Of course! Let me show you. They're just over here.
choices.reading: of COURSE! let me SHOW you. they're JUST over HERE.
choices.feedback: Helpful, polite and natural customer service.
choices.why: 'Let me show you' and 'just over here' are friendly, helpful phrases in shops.

choices.feedback: He'll find them, but it's very blunt for customer service.
choices.why: With customers, soften directions: 'They're just over there, on the left.'

choices.feedback: Too casual, and unhelpful! Offer to check: 'Let me check for you.'
choices.why: If you don't know, say 'Let me check for you' or 'I'll ask my manager'.

survival.title: Weekend shift
survival.context: Ms. Clarke is planning next week's rota.

steps.speaker: clarke
steps.translation: Are you able to work on Saturday?

choices.text: I'm sorry, I can't this Saturday. I have a class.
choices.reading: I'm SOR-ry, I CAN'T this SAT-ur-day. I HAVE a CLASS.
choices.translation: Sorry, I'm not free this Saturday because of a class.
choices.feedback: A polite 'no' with a reason. Very natural.
choices.why: English softens refusals with 'I'm sorry' and a short reason.

choices.feedback: Clear, but very abrupt. Add 'I'm sorry' and a short reason.
choices.why: A bare 'No' to your manager can sound rude. 'Sorry, I can't, I have a class' is much better.

choices.feedback: That's past tense: 'I worked on Saturday'. She's asking about THIS Saturday.
choices.why: 'Could you work…?' is about the future. Answer 'I can' or 'I can't'.

survival.title: Ask a coworker
survival.context: Priya checks on you during your shift.

steps.speaker: priya
steps.translation: Is there anything you want to ask?

choices.text: Yeah, where do the new books go?
choices.reading: YEAH, WHERE do the NEW BOOKS GO?
choices.translation: Yes: where should I put the new books?
choices.feedback: Casual and specific. Perfect with a friendly coworker.
choices.why: With friends at work, short casual questions are natural.

choices.translation: (Very formal) Yes, I have a question.
choices.feedback: Way too formal for Priya, and you didn't say what you need!
choices.why: 'Indeed' and 'query' are formal. With coworkers, just ask the question.

choices.feedback: Honest! But a specific question gets you better help.
choices.why: Ask about one concrete thing (where, how, when): it's easier for people to help.

survival.title: Wrong book
survival.context: You gave a customer the wrong book.

steps.speaker: leo
steps.text: Sorry, this isn't the book I ordered.
steps.reading: SOR-ry, this ISN'T the BOOK I OR-dered.
steps.translation: This is not the book I asked for.

choices.text: I'm so sorry about that. Let me get the right one for you.
choices.reading: I'm SO SOR-ry a-BOUT THAT. let me GET the RIGHT one for YOU.
choices.translation: I apologise. I'll bring the correct book.
choices.feedback: A clear apology plus a fix. Excellent.
choices.why: In customer service: apologise first ('I'm so sorry about that'), then solve it ('Let me…').

choices.feedback: Too casual for a customer. Use 'I'm so sorry about that'.
choices.why: 'Mate' is for friends. With customers, keep it polite and helpful.

choices.translation: Yes, it is the right book.
choices.feedback: Arguing with the customer! Apologise and fix it.
choices.why: Even if you're not sure, check politely: 'Let me check that for you.'
